36.0.s.en: (1) Esau's wives and children in Canaan

36.0.0.en: Three wives of Esau are mentioned here, and other lists of the names of Esau's wives are found in (ch. 26:34, ch. 28:9). Some differences in the names can be noticed, because each woman had more than one name. The first wife, Adah, is also called Bashemath; Aholibamah has another name, Judith, and her father's name is Anah, who also has another name, Beeri. The name of her grandfather Zibeon is also mentioned, to whom she is likewise ascribed as a daughter, since a granddaughter is regarded as a daughter. He is called Zibeon the Hivite, although elsewhere it says Beeri the Hittite; both belong to the Canaanite tribes, which could intermarry, for their origin is Hivite and Hittite. As for Bashemath the daughter of Ishmael, she has another name, Mahalath.

36.0.1.en: A person's name is of great value to him, so benefit from your name, if it has a special meaning, in order to live by it, for it may be a message from God to you.

36.1.0.en: Five sons were born to Esau in Canaan, while he was living with his father Isaac. The first was Eliphaz, by Adah, and the meaning of his name is God is his strength.

36.1.1.en: The second was Reuel, by Bashemath, and the meaning of his name is God's care.

36.2.0.en: Three sons were born by Aholibamah, who are:

36.2.1.en: Jeush: its meaning is God hastens.

36.2.2.en: The second, Jaalam: its meaning is God knows.

36.2.3.en: The third, Korah: its meaning is the gourd plant.

36.2.4.en: These formed tribes far from the people of God and from the faith, but many of them returned afterward to faith in Christ.

36.3.0.en: When Jacob received the blessing from his father Isaac, and Esau became sure that Jacob was the only heir of the land of Canaan, he felt that it would not hold both of them with all their possessions, so he moved south toward the mountains of Seir. It was called by this name because of its many trees, for the word Seir means thick hair. And Esau, meaning hairy, was also called Edom, meaning red, because his skin tended to redness in addition to being hairy.

36.4.0.en: The grandchildren of Esau are mentioned here: he had six grandsons by Eliphaz and four grandsons by Reuel, and his grandchildren by his three sons born of Aholibamah are not mentioned.

36.5.0.en: The sons and grandsons of Esau became dukes, that is, chiefs of tribes. It is noticeable that Korah his son by Aholibamah is mentioned a second time with his grandsons by Eliphaz, because he was related to them by marriage and shared with them in moving and in work.

36.5.1.en: Many tribes came forth from Esau, but they departed from the faith because of their distance from Jacob, and they were occupied with their many sons and possessions. Do not be preoccupied with the strength of your children and their number, or with the abundance of possessions, for all of them pass away; rather care for your faith in God and the faith of your family, which shows itself in love for God and for those around you.

37.0.0.en: Moses the prophet tells us of the rest of Jacob's life, and the most important person who appears is his son Joseph. It is mentioned here that he was seventeen years old and was helping his brothers, the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, in tending the flock; perhaps Bilhah, his mother's maidservant, became like a mother to him after Rachel's death.

37.0.1.en: Joseph was the best of his brothers in his life and spiritual conduct, in his love and in his obedience to his father, while his brothers were wicked and spoke evil words about their father and about many people. So Joseph brought this evil report to his father so that he would watch over them and discipline them, and also so that he might guard against their evils. He was not proud, nor did he seek any personal gain, but wanted them to turn back from their errors, as proved by all the coming events, which will show his good feelings toward them.

37.1.0.en: Because of Joseph's distinction in love and spirituality, his father loved him and gave him a coat of many colors, a garment worn over the clothes like a cloak, worn by distinguished people and giving an appearance of greatness. The coat was an expression of Jacob's love, but at the same time it aroused his brothers' jealousy instead of moving them to imitate him. In their distress at their father's love for him, his brothers treated him harshly and spoke evil words to him that showed their hatred of him. Joseph is a type of Christ, and the coat of the Church, which He wears on His body, while the colors signify the variety of the gifts of the members of the Church.

37.1.1.en: If you see a distinguished person, try to learn a virtue from him, and keep away from jealousy and envy, which ruin your soul and corrupt your relationship with others.

37.2.0.en: A dream: dreams are either the product of what is stored in the subconscious, that is, the events that have passed through a person, which is the case with most people's dreams, or they are from God and have spiritual meanings, as in the case of Joseph. God supported Joseph with dreams so that he could bear his brothers' wrongs against him. His first dream was that he was with his brothers binding sheaves in the field, and each of them bound what he had gathered in a sheaf, and his sheaf, which he had set on the ground, arose and stood upright, while the sheaves of his brothers gathered round about it, at its feet, as if bowing down to it. When his brothers heard the divine dream, instead of ceasing their hatred of him and honoring him, since God was glorifying him, they became more distressed with him, because he would have dominion over them.

37.3.0.en: Your mother: he means Bilhah, Zilpah and Leah, who stood in the place of his mother.

37.3.1.en: Joseph saw a second dream, that the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to him. His brothers were all the more angered at him, and his father also rebuked him, but inwardly he believed in his son's standing and the glory awaiting him, and kept the matter carefully within himself.

37.3.2.en: May you understand and learn from the events around you what builds you up spiritually and binds you to God; that is, draw out God's message to you from everything you hear, so that you may grow in your spiritual life.

37.4.s.en: (2) Jacob sends Joseph to his brothers

37.4.0.en: Joseph's ten older brothers went out to feed the flock and headed north to the region of Shechem, where they used to dwell, while Joseph and Benjamin, the young ones, their father kept with him at home because of their youth.

37.5.0.en: Jacob was anxious about his sons because of their delay in Shechem. Perhaps he feared for them from the tribes around the place, lest they take revenge on them for what they had done some time before when they killed the tribe of Shechem (ch. 34). So he asked Joseph to go and see about his brothers and ask how they were, and he obeyed at once.

37.5.1.en: Be quick in your obedience to God and to those around you, even if the request is hard or urgent, because by your obedience you show your love for others and give up your own comfort, and your standing increases, not only with them but also with God.

37.6.0.en: The vale of Hebron: the low region near the city of Hebron in the south of Canaan. Jacob sent his son Joseph to ask how his brothers were, and their flocks that they were tending.

37.7.0.en: Dothan: it means two wells, and it is nine miles northeast of Samaria and twelve miles from Shechem.

37.7.1.en: Joseph arrived, with some food, to ask about his brothers in Shechem, but he did not find them. He began to look for them left and right, and a man of that place found him wandering, and asked him what he was seeking. He told him that he was looking for his ten brothers who used to feed their flocks in that place. The man told him that he had indeed seen them, and informed him that they had gone to Dothan. So Joseph traveled until he came to Dothan and found them there.

37.7.2.en: Be persevering in your service until you complete it, however tired you are, and do not make excuses for yourself and leave the souls you serve to be lost. Care for those around you even if they wrong you, and seek the salvation and comfort of their souls, and you will win them in the end.

37.8.s.en: (3) Joseph is cast into the pit

37.8.0.en: They conspired against him: they plotted against him.

37.8.1.en: Joseph's feelings were love and concern for his brothers, but when they saw him from afar they thought among themselves how they might kill him, to be rid of his dreams and of God's blessing upon him, instead of submitting to God, honoring their brother and following his good conduct. So they agreed to kill him and cast him into one of the pits, and then lie to their father and claim that a wild beast had devoured him in the wilderness.

37.8.2.en: Sin leads to another sin after it. Jealousy led to hatred, and hatred to malice and revenge, and the last to persistence in killing and then lying. Do not be lax with the smallest sin, lest it lead you to dreadful evils, and hasten to repentance and to examining yourself day by day.

37.9.0.en: Reuben the firstborn intervened to save Joseph from being killed. Perhaps he felt his responsibility before his father, when he would ask him for his brother and why he had not kept him safe. So he proposed to his brothers that they cast him into one of the dry pits, so that when they left the pit he could take him out and bring him back to his father.

37.10.0.en: Joseph reached his brothers, and instead of welcoming him they fell upon him, snatched the food he had with him, and angrily stripped off his coat of many colors, and then cast him into a dry pit that was near them.

37.11.0.en: Ishmaelites: that is, descendants of Ishmael, the son of Abraham; but in (v. 28) it calls them Midianites, that is, descendants of Midian, who was also a son of Abraham, by Keturah. The two tribes intermarried, and these traveling merchants resulted, so that their origin is from Ishmael and Midian.

37.11.1.en: Gilead: it lies east of the Jordan, where Laban and Jacob agreed that neither would harm the other, and they set up the heap of witness (ch. 31:48). Spicery: a kind of gum that comes from the tragacanth tree, also used in medicine.

37.11.2.en: Balm: a sweet-smelling ointment produced from the balsam plant and used in medicine and embalming.

37.11.3.en: Myrrh (ladanum): a kind of gum, also used in medicine.

37.11.4.en: After Joseph was cast into the pit, his brothers sat down to eat of the food he had brought them from their father, with an astonishing hardness of heart. And as they ate, they looked from afar and saw a caravan of merchants coming from Gilead and going to Egypt, carrying gums and sweet-smelling ointments to sell there.

37.12.0.en: When Judah saw the caravan of merchants, he had compassion on Joseph and proposed to his brothers that they sell him to the caravan, so that they would be rid of him without needing to kill him, because he was their brother. Thus their hearts were softened toward him, and they agreed to his proposal.

37.13.0.en: They drew Joseph up out of the pit and sold him to the merchants for twenty pieces of silver. Twenty pieces of silver: that is, twenty shekels, and the shekel is about 15 grams.

37.14.0.en: Reuben had gone far away to do some work while they were eating and selling their brother to the merchants. When he came back, he looked for him in the pit and did not find him, and he was troubled and asked them about him. They told him what they had done, and he was deeply grieved and said to them, What shall I say to my father? That is, I have no answer or explanation for Joseph's disappearance.

37.15.1.en: Joseph's brothers hid their crime by killing a kid of the goats and staining Joseph's coat with its blood, and they sent it, by one of the servants or one of themselves, to their father, telling him that they had found this coat in the wilderness and asking him to determine whether it was Joseph's coat or not, intending to make their father believe that Joseph was dead.

37.15.2.en: If you sin, repent of your sin so that God may forgive it, and do not persist in it and try to hide it with other sins such as lying, lest you anger God and stir up people against you.

37.16.0.en: Sackcloth: a coarse black cloth made of goat's hair.

37.16.1.en: Loins: the sides of his thighs. The meaning is that the sackcloth was worn from the waist and hung down over the sides of the thighs. When Jacob examined the coat, he was certain that it was Joseph's, and understood from the blood that a wild beast had devoured him in the wilderness. So he wept much for him and rent his clothes, an ancient and well-known sign of great grief, and put on coarse cloth, which is sackcloth, as a sign of abasement. His sons and daughters tried to calm his grief but could not; rather he said, I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning. Hades, or the abyss, was the meeting place of all the departed, because Christ had not yet accomplished redemption.

37.17.0.en: Potiphar: a name connected with Ra, the sun god.

37.17.1.en: Officer (eunuch): either he was in fact one of the eunuchs, or, according to another opinion, it had become a title given to those of high rank in the service of the king of Egypt. So either he was a eunuch and had a wife who lived with him as a sister, or he was an ordinary married man and this was merely a title for him.

37.17.2.en: Pharaoh: most probably one of the kings of the fifteenth or sixteenth dynasty, and most probably one of the Hyksos, who occupied some places in Egypt and are called the Shepherd Kings.

37.17.3.en: Captain of the guard: the one responsible for security in Egypt, like a minister of the interior, and also responsible for the prisons.

37.17.4.en: The merchants reached Egypt and sold their goods and the slaves they had with them, and Potiphar bought Joseph to be a servant to him.

37.17.5.en: We notice in this chapter that Joseph is a type of Christ in many respects, which will be gathered at the end of chapter fifty.

38.0.0.en: An Adullamite: from the city of Adullam, one of the great cities of Canaan, lying near Bethlehem. Judah the son of Jacob went to visit a person who seems to have been his friend, called Hirah, a pagan man who lived in one of the cities of Canaan called Adullam.

38.1.0.en: While Judah was in the city of Adullam, where he stayed a while in the house of his friend Hirah, his eyes wandered and he was taken with a girl, and his desire was stirred toward her, and he married her although she was a pagan, the daughter of a man named Shuah.

38.1.1.en: Beware of mixing with those far from God and of leaving your senses lax, lest they draw you into a conduct and life far from God. If you become bound to lusts, your way to repentance becomes harder than before. Do not cling to sin and grow accustomed to it, lest you sell your Christ and then regret it afterward when you have become weak.

38.2.0.en: This pagan woman bore Judah three sons, Er and Onan, and after some years he went to the city of Chezib, which lies in the south of Palestine, and she bore a third son, whom she called Shelah.

38.2.1.en: Judah was preoccupied with and delighted in lust and in having many sons, and of course he lived several years among the pagans and was affected by their ways. He did not know that all he had done was vanity, distancing him from God, since his last son was born in Chezib, whose meaning is lie. This signifies that all he had obtained of sons and lust was a lie and without value; yet God turns our vain works into the greatest thing, since Christ humbled Himself and came from the offspring of Judah and of Tamar the pagan, who will be mentioned shortly.

38.3.s.en: (2) The marriage of Judah's two sons

38.3.0.en: Judah was still living among the pagans, and his firstborn son Er grew up, so he gave him a pagan girl called Tamar. But the character of his son Er was wicked, because his mother was a pagan and he lived among wicked pagans. God gave him the chance to learn faith from his father and to live with God, but he persisted in evil and died while young.

38.4.0.en: Judah asked his second son Onan to marry Tamar, the wife of his brother Er who had died, so that he might raise up offspring to his brother and then to himself. For it was the custom in that time that if a brother died without children, his brother married his wife, and the firstborn son was counted as the son of the dead man so that his name would not be blotted out, while the sons after him were counted to the living husband. The Law of Moses later laid this down (Deut 25:5), all in expectation of the Messiah, the Savior. This has no meaning now after the coming of the Messiah, for Christianity forbids the marriage of a brother to the wife of his dead brother, because she is regarded as his sister, and what matters now is spiritual virtues and preparation for eternity, not the begetting of children.

38.5.0.en: Onan was selfish and loved money, though he was a young man, as a result of his wicked upbringing. He did not want the inheritance to be shared by three brothers, but to be for himself and for Shelah his young brother only, so he did not want to beget children by Tamar. So when he was joined to her bodily, he took care that this should not lead to a complete relationship and the begetting of offspring. God was angry with him because of his persistence in evil and greed, and he died also.

38.5.1.en: Do not be attached to money and passing material things, lest they gain control over you and lead you to wicked deeds, so that you provoke God's anger and lose every blessing in your life, and grieve in your worldly life and in the life to come.

38.6.1.en: Judah did not take heed of his sin in clinging to the wicked and begetting wicked sons, and he was still thinking of material fruits, that is, having offspring called by his name from his sons. But there was no small difference in age between Onan and Shelah; that is, Shelah was a child who could not marry. So Judah told his daughter-in-law Tamar to remain in her father's house until Shelah grew up, and he would give her to him. But in truth fear had begun to control him about Shelah's death, for some people, by a mistaken belief, suppose that a wife may sometimes be the cause of trouble to whomever she marries, because of their pagan beliefs in bad luck, omens and pessimism. So he feared for his son's death, and perhaps he wanted to save him from it and keep him away from marrying Tamar; that is, he was lying in his promise to Tamar to give her to Shelah.

38.6.2.en: Judah's mind was polluted by evil and by the thoughts of the pagans. So be careful in what you see or hear and in all your relationships, and do not promise anything you cannot guarantee; rather let your heart be pure and your promises true, and you will receive God's blessing.

38.7.0.en: The Canaanite woman, Judah's wife, the daughter of Shuah, died, and after the mourning Judah's heart was comforted, and he went up to a town called Timnath, lying west of Jerusalem, where he had sheep. The season of sheep-shearing came, so he went to oversee the shearers, and Tamar his daughter-in-law heard that he was going to Timnath.

38.8.0.en: Tamar was troubled because Judah had not fulfilled his promise to give her his son Shelah as a husband, although he had grown up, in order to raise up offspring to her dead husband Er. She was, like any woman, hoping that the Messiah, the Savior, would come from her offspring, as God had promised Eve and then Abraham.

38.8.1.en: So she thought of a ruse to raise up offspring for herself. She put off her widow's garments, which were most likely dark or black, and put on bright clothes, covered her face with a veil, and sat on the road to the city of Timnath, where Judah would pass, in a place called Enaim, whose meaning is two eyes. Her appearance was like that of a professional harlot, of those who devote themselves to fornication to please the goddess Ashtoreth, and who cover their faces and wait on the roads to commit fornication with whoever passes by them. And Judah indeed passed by on the road and saw her, and understood that she was one of the harlots, and did not know that she was his daughter-in-law, because her face was covered.

38.9.0.en: Lust was stirred in Judah's heart, so he asked Tamar, not knowing her, to lie with him. She asked him for payment, as one of the professional harlots, and he promised to give her a kid. She asked him to give her a pledge, that is, a guarantee or proof that he would fulfill the promise. He said to her, What pledge shall I give you? She asked for his signet, and his bracelets, a piece of cloth wound around the head like a turban, and also his staff. He gave her what she asked, and lay with her, and she conceived. Afterward she returned and put on her widow's garments and lived in her house.

38.9.1.en: We must not fail to add here that whatever Tamar's motive or grief, a spiritual person must never resort to a wrong way to attain a lawful or noble end. A sound goal must be reached by a sound way, and it would have been better for Tamar to pray and believe in God, who is able to do her justice.

38.10.0.en: Let her take it to her: she is responsible for not taking her payment, that is, the kid, and let her take for herself the pledge that he left with her.

38.10.1.en: We shall be shamed: so that no one may shame us for not having paid the wages.

38.10.2.en: After Judah went to Timnath, he sent the kid by his friend the Adullamite to Enaim to give the harlot her payment, but he did not find her. He asked about her, and the people of the place denied that there was a harlot who used to sit there. So he returned with the kid to Judah, who said, Let her take the pledge to her, and I am not responsible, and I have not failed to give her the payment.

38.11.0.en: After three months the signs of pregnancy began to appear on Tamar, and when her neighbors learned of it they were very troubled and told her father-in-law Judah, who was angry and decided that she should die by burning with fire, and he came to carry out the sentence of death upon her. When they brought her out to be burned, she said to Judah before those gathered, Whose are these? By the man whose these are, am I with child. And she brought out the pledge, that is, the signet, the bracelets and the staff. When Judah looked at her he was ashamed of himself, and declared before the people of the city that she was innocent, indeed more righteous than he, because he had failed in his promise and had not given her his son Shelah, and he was responsible for her, because he was the one who had lain with her. So he took her to his house, to be a wife to him, and moreover to keep her and support her and the one in her womb. And the chastity of this woman appeared before all, for she did not seek her lust but only the begetting of offspring, so she lay with this old man.

38.11.1.en: Do not be hasty in judging others, lest they be more righteous than you. Do not judge, that you be not judged, and try to make excuses however clear and great the faults are. At least say to yourself that all people are weak, and pray for all, or at least pray for yourself, for you may be weaker than they.
